aid-cover-for-spies.title_asserts: Rich governments use their aid programmes as cover for intelligence operations inside other countries.
aid-cover-for-spies.why: The individual episodes are on the record and one of them was effectively conceded by the US government, but each is a separate exposed instance rather than evidence of a standing practice. The best-sourced document here is a senator's 1992 statement in the Congressional Record releasing a GAO report, which says intelligence agencies had 'an important role' in the police-training programmes; that is a senator's characterisation, not an official finding that aid was used as cover. The Timor-Leste bugging remains an allegation Australia has never admitted, and USAID says ZunZuneo was not covert, so what is unresolved is exactly what HYP calls a suspected pattern: whether this is design or four accidents of exposure.
aid-cover-for-spies.still_open: Whether intelligence use of aid cover is continuing practice rather than four exposed episodes; whether ASIS used the Dili aid project as cover (Australia has never admitted it); what the USAID inspector general found on ZunZuneo in 2014.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: Congressional Record, 5 March 1992: Senator Cranston releasing the GAO report 'Foreign Aid: Police Training and Assistance'. Gives the 1974 section 660 ban, 'a dozen exemptions', $60 million a year training police in 34 countries by 1968 through the AID Office of Public Safety, and the claim that US intelligence agencies had an important role in those programmes.

aid-into-offshore-accounts.title_asserts: Money given and lent to poor countries ends up in Swiss bank accounts.
aid-into-offshore-accounts.narrower_title: Aid payments matched, quarter for quarter, by jumps in secret-haven bank deposits
aid-into-offshore-accounts.why: The World Bank's own working paper, which I opened, establishes the statistical fact in the narrower title and nothing beyond it: it says only that its findings are “suggestive of aid diversion”, not that diversion occurred. The paper cannot name an account, a person or a transfer, and the entry's own third paragraph concedes this. So the measured association is documented; the claim that aid money turns up in named officials' Swiss accounts is not.

settled_by.what_it_is: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9150, 'Elite Capture of Foreign Aid: Evidence from Offshore Bank Accounts' (Andersen, Johannesen, Rijkers), full text on the Bank's own document server; later published in the Journal of Political Economy
settled_by.what_it_establishes: In the 22 most aid-dependent countries, a quarter in which a country receives aid worth 1% of GDP coincides with haven deposits rising 3.4%, with no rise in non-havens; implied leakage about 7.5% at the sample mean and about 5% of aggregate disbursements; Switzerland and Luxembourg contribute significantly, Belgium and Jersey do not.

aid-into-offshore-accounts.still_open: Whose money it is; whether the rise is theft, legitimate transfers or something else, which the authors say they cannot tell; whether the same holds for IMF, regional-bank and bilateral disbursements; why the Bank held the paper back in 2019-20.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: Full text of WPS 9150, including abstract, the 3.4% estimate and the derivation of the 7.5% and 5% leakage rates.

rankings-bent-for-money.title_asserts: The World Bank's global rankings were altered in favour of countries whose money the institution wanted.
rankings-bent-for-money.why: This is the shape REVIEW42 names: an outside law firm engaged by the Bank itself, which collected five million documents and interviewed more than three dozen staff, found that published data was changed for China in Doing Business 2018 and for Saudi Arabia in Doing Business 2020, and tied both to money - China's data was changed during the capital increase campaign, and the Saudi change was found likely to have been made to reward Saudi Arabia for its paid advisory contracts with the Bank. Two editions, two paying or capital-contributing countries, plus the Bank's decision to cancel the product: that is the practice existing, not a single anecdote. The report's own counter-example matters and sits in still_open.

settled_by.what_it_is: WilmerHale, 'Investigation of Data Irregularities in Doing Business 2018 and Doing Business 2020: Investigation Findings and Report to the Board of Executive Directors', commissioned by the IBRD and published on the World Bank's own document server
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Improper changes to data for China (DB2018) and Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Azerbaijan (DB2020). China's final report had been approved at rank 85, seven places down on the prior year; after changes directed through the president's office and after CEO Georgieva told the DEC director to “wrap this up”, China was published at 78. On Saudi Arabia the report concludes the change was likely an effort by a senior staff member to reward the country for its RAS projects, the Bank's paid advisory contracts.

rankings-bent-for-money.still_open: Whether the other seventeen editions were also changed, and whether this happens in the Bank's other rankings. The same report cuts against the money framing in one place: Azerbaijan's data was changed downward because Mr Djankov personally disbelieved its reforms and, the report says, appeared to harbour a personal animus against the country, which is not a money motive. The full original-and-final data for every country and edition, with each change and its requester, is still unpublished.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The WilmerHale report in full: paragraphs 3-18 on China, 19-23 on Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Azerbaijan, and 33-36 on motive.

routes_that_failed.how_it_failed: HTTP 403; the entry's own copy of the WilmerHale report would not download. The Bank's own copy served and was used instead.

ports-that-become-naval-bases.title_asserts: Some ports China has financed may become naval bases in future.
ports-that-become-naval-bases.why: The title is hedged with 'may' and the record matches that hedge exactly. Djibouti and Ream are documented as Chinese-built facilities now used by China's navy, but the claim about the other ports is a forecast, and the researchers who made the shortlist present it as inference, not finding - their chapter is titled 'Reading the tea leaves' and they note that none of the ports is currently militarily defensible. What is unresolved is intent and design, which is what suspected is for.
ports-that-become-naval-bases.still_open: Whether port lending was designed with naval use in mind. The concession and loan contracts for the eight shortlisted ports are unpublished, and there is no consolidated record of naval port calls to test the forecast against.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: AidData, 'Harboring Global Ambitions' (2023). Confirms the entry's figures: 123 seaport projects worth $29.9 billion at 78 ports in 46 countries, 2000-2021; the eight-port shortlist in the order given in the entry; and the statement that none of the ports described is currently militarily defensible.

carbon-credits-new-land-grab.title_asserts: The carbon credit market is causing a new wave of land seizures in poor countries.
carbon-credits-new-land-grab.narrower_title: Huge areas signed over for carbon credits, and a flagship carbon project's land taken without consent
carbon-credits-new-land-grab.why: The scale of the agreements and the unlawfulness of one flagship project's land-taking are documented, including by a Kenyan court. The causal step in the title is not: on the opening case the government says it was protecting the forest, Blue Carbon says it had no project in Kenya, and an AFP investigation found the African deals largely went nowhere, which cuts against credits driving the evictions. No count exists of carbon projects overlapping documented evictions, so the link between the market and the seizures remains the suspicion.

settled_by.what_it_is: Osman & 164 others v Northern Rangelands Trust & 8 others (Environment and Land Court, Petition 006 of 2021), as recorded in the Sabin Center climate litigation database
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The court found the conservancies were established in breach of public participation, that conservancy activities operated outside the legal framework and infringed property rights, and that armed rangers operated illegally; it blocked establishment in Chari and Cherab and halted the Bulesa Biliqo conservancy.

carbon-credits-new-land-grab.still_open: Whether carbon finance caused the Ogiek evictions or any other eviction; whether the signed agreements become projects at all. And the 31 January 2025 judgment is not final - Kenya Law's index lists a Court of Appeal ruling in Northern Rangelands Trust's appeal (Civil Appeal (Application) E019 of 2026) on 25 September 2026, which the story does not mention.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: Kenya Law's judgment search index: shows the Osman petition against Northern Rangelands Trust and, at [2026] KECA 1774, a Court of Appeal ruling of 25 September 2026 in the Trust's appeal.
Case record giving the judgment date of 31 January 2025 and the holdings and reliefs granted.

routes_that_failed.how_it_failed: HTTP 202 with an empty body - the judgment pages are behind a challenge, as REVIEW42 warned. Same for /akn/ke/judgment/keca/2026/1774/eng@2026-09-25. Not pursued further.

bribes-built-into-financed-contracts.title_asserts: Bribes are a built-in component of the contracts that development loans pay for.
bribes-built-into-financed-contracts.narrower_title: Bribes paid to win the contracts that development loans finance
bribes-built-into-financed-contracts.why: The lender's own sanctions system settles more than instances: in fiscal 2024 alone the World Bank Group imposed about 35 debarments, six of them on grounds including corruption, on projects in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Iraq, Somalia, Viet Nam and the DRC, and it publishes a new set every year. Together with the Lesotho convictions that is a recurring, lender-found practice, not an anecdote. What the debarments and convictions do not establish is the title's extra step - that the bribe is built into the contract price and so repaid by the borrower with interest. Nobody has compared prices on lender-financed contracts with the same firms' unfinanced work.

settled_by.what_it_is: World Bank Group Sanctions System Data Companion, fiscal year 2024, prepared by the Sanctions Board Secretariat and the Office of Suspension and Debarment
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Firm-by-firm debarments imposed in one year on Bank-financed projects with 'Corruption' or 'Fraud and Corruption' as the stated ground, including M/S Gul Construction (Pakistan), BETS Consulting Services (Bangladesh), Marseille for Engineering & Trading (Iraq), Ernst & Young LLP (Kenya, on a Somalia project) and TPF Getinsa Euroestudios (Spain, on a Viet Nam project).

bribes-built-into-financed-contracts.still_open: Whether bribes are priced into financed contracts and passed to the borrower; what the Bank's investigation files behind each debarment contain; what share of financed contracts involve payments that were never found.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The FY2024 debarment tables; I counted the rows and the corruption grounds within them.

routes_that_failed.how_it_failed: HTTP 401, subscription key required - the machine-readable debarment list is not open, so a running total of corruption debarments across all years could not be taken.

seed-laws-for-seed-companies.title_asserts: Seed laws that restrict farmers' use of their own seed are being pushed on poor countries by the lenders.
seed-laws-for-seed-companies.narrower_title: World Bank rankings and loan conditions that favour the commercial seed system
seed-laws-for-seed-companies.why: The Bank's own documents establish the narrower claim. Its 2017 agriculture ranking scored countries on the “existence, duration and terms of plant variety protection” and on seed certification practice, and its own seed indicator page says the measure focuses on the formal sector. Two of the loan documents CAFOD links, both Bank completion reports I opened, confirm prior actions tying agricultural loans to subsidised hybrid seed and fertiliser in Kenya and Guinea. The part of the title that is not documented by any document I could open is the central one: that seed certification laws restricting farmers' seed were required as loan conditions. That rests on CAFOD's own trawl of Bank files, and CAFOD links no document for the seven countries it names.

settled_by.what_it_is: World Bank, 'Enabling the Business of Agriculture 2017', the Bank's own ranking report
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Table 2.1 scores the seed topic on the existence, duration and terms of plant variety protection, the right to license protected varieties and seed certification arrangements, and the text treats new plant variety protection laws, as adopted in Burundi and Rwanda that year, as improvement. The report also explains that UPOV membership requires a country's law to conform to the 1991 Act.

settled_by.what_it_is: World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005801 (Kenya development policy operation) and ICR00006096 (Guinea), the two Bank documents CAFOD links for its first finding
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Prior actions for budget-support loans built on e-voucher schemes distributing subsidised inputs, described in Kenya as “seeds, fertilizers, training” and in Guinea as improved seeds, fertilizers and herbicides, with measures to enlist private agro-dealers.

seed-laws-for-seed-companies.still_open: Whether seed certification laws were prior actions for loans to the Central African Republic, Chad, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Mozambique and Nigeria, as CAFOD reports; who drafted the laws that followed; whether foreign seed companies' market share rose afterwards. Also unverified: the entry's opening claim that the Bank held Tanzania up as a model in 2016 for joining UPOV 1991 - I did not open the 2016 edition.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The Bank's own supplying-seed indicator page, which matches the entry's paragraph 3 paraphrase almost word for word.
Enabling the Business of Agriculture 2017 in full, including the seed indicator table and the UPOV explanation.
Kenya DPO completion report, prior actions on the subsidised-input e-voucher programme.
Guinea DPO completion report, same kind of prior action.
The CAFOD head of policy's piece, which is where the two prior-action findings and the linked loan documents come from.

routes_that_failed.how_it_failed: HTTP 404, as did two other UPOV paths, so the 1991 Act's own text on farm-saved seed was not opened; the restriction on farmers' seed therefore still rests on secondary accounts.

vulture-funds.title_asserts: Hedge funds buy poor countries' debt cheaply and sue in rich-country courts for its full value.
vulture-funds.why: The documented pattern already on the page states this entry's whole claim and counts it: the ECB working paper it is built on, which I opened, finds 158 suits against 34 defaulting governments, 130 of them in US courts, and describes funds that “buy debt at a discount and then sue for full repayment”, with two-thirds of new cases now brought by hedge funds. The page's pattern also carries Argentina's $10 billion holdout payout, Elliott and Peru, asset seizures and the New York bills. Nothing load-bearing in the entry is missing from it.
vulture-funds.left_over_after_the_duplicate: Four things the existing pattern does not carry: that the targets include countries receiving debt relief (Donegal v Zambia, and the UN independent expert's count of 54 suits against 12 heavily indebted poor countries from 1998 to 2008); the ARA Libertad seizure in Ghana in 2012 as a vivid instance; Hamilton Reserve v Sri Lanka in 2022, which falls after the ECB paper's 2010 cut-off; and the UK's 2010 Act and Belgium's 2015 law limiting what such funds can recover from the poorest countries, against which the pattern only records New York's failed bills. If the owner wants this kept as a suspicion, the one part still genuinely open is whether the business depends on blocking debt relief, since purchase prices are not disclosed.

settled_by.what_it_is: ECB Working Paper No. 2135, 'Sovereign defaults in court' (Schumacher, Trebesch, Enderlein)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: 158 litigation cases against 34 defaulting sovereigns, 1976-2010, filed in the US or UK; since 2000, 65% brought by distressed debt funds; of 148 cases with a known creditor, 79 were filed by funds; the paper describes funds that buy at a discount and sue for full repayment.

vulture-funds.still_open: What the funds paid for the debt, and therefore the true size of their returns; whether suing is a strategy that depends on other creditors granting relief.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The ECB working paper underpinning the documented pattern, checked for the 158 cases, the 65% share and the buy-at-a-discount description.
Read only, to get the full text of the holdout-funds-rich-courts pattern, which the batch file supplies truncated.

private-equity-with-development-money.title_asserts: Development money is handed to private equity funds and to for-profit hospitals.
private-equity-with-development-money.why: The title asserts the channel, not the harm, and the channel is published by the institutions themselves and audited by a government watchdog. The UK's Independent Commission for Aid Impact, reporting to Parliament, records that CDC invests “through private equity funds” alongside direct investment and that health was 7% of its portfolio, £258.8 million, at the end of 2017. The development banks' own statements that they put about $200 million into the Abraaj health fund and hired forensic accountants to look for it are not in dispute either. The harm claims in the entry's conviction line are a different and narrower matter, and they belong in still_open.

settled_by.what_it_is: Independent Commission for Aid Impact, 'CDC's investments in low-income and fragile states: a performance review', a review by a statutory body reporting to the UK Parliament
settled_by.what_it_establishes: That UK aid's development finance institution invests through private equity funds as one of its products (17% of new investments between 2012 and Q3 2017, with intermediated equity 23-37% of the portfolio) and in healthcare businesses; and, on the question the entry raises, that for an Indian healthcare fund the investment papers did not consider which groups would benefit, that CDC later said the funded services had largely reached those on above-average incomes, and that papers for more than three-quarters of the sample ignored the question.

private-equity-with-development-money.still_open: Whether money is routinely skimmed - Abraaj is one collapse and one set of US charges, not a measured pattern; what management fees the funds take; who the patients at funded hospitals actually are, since no fund-level disclosure or independent patient-income data exists.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The ICAI performance review in full, read for the fund-investment shares, the sector table and the findings on who benefited.

routes_that_failed.how_it_failed: Page served but is a JavaScript application with no readable content and no discoverable data endpoint, so IFC's own disclosure for the Abraaj health fund could not be read.
HTTP 302 to an unusable location; the IFC investment dataset could not be queried for Abraaj.

companies-pay-armed-groups.title_asserts: Foreign companies pay soldiers and militias to protect their operations abroad.
companies-pay-armed-groups.why: Two things carry this past the single-instance bar. One multinational pleaded guilty in a US federal court to over 100 payments totalling more than $1.7 million to a designated paramilitary group, booked in its own records as “security payments”, and kept paying after the Justice Department told it the payments were illegal; a second company's guilty plea in 2022 covers payments to armed groups in Syria. And a third company states in its current annual report to the SEC that it pays support costs for government-provided security including allowances to the military and police - a continuing practice the company defends rather than denies. A guilty plea settles its own instance; a standing disclosure in a 10-K settles that the payments are ordinary business for that company, and two pleas plus a live disclosure across three continents settle that the practice exists.

settled_by.what_it_is: US Department of Justice press release 07-161, on Chiquita Brands International's guilty plea before the US District Court for the District of Columbia
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Over 100 payments totalling more than $1.7 million to the AUC from 1997 to 4 February 2004 through the subsidiary Banadex, recorded in its books as security payments; 50 payments of over $825,000 after the group was designated; 20 payments of over $300,000 after Chiquita disclosed to the Justice Department and was told they were illegal; a $25 million fine. The release also notes Chiquita never received any actual security services.

settled_by.what_it_is: Freeport-McMoRan Inc. annual report on Form 10-K for 2025, filed with the SEC
settled_by.what_it_establishes: In the company's own words, “PTFI pays support costs for government-provided security”: food, housing, fuel, travel, vehicle repairs, allowances for incidental and administrative costs, and community programmes carried out by the military and police, which it calls a prudent response to protecting its workforce and property.

companies-pay-armed-groups.still_open: Whether this is routine across companies in conflict areas rather than documented at a handful of large ones - there is no mandatory disclosure of payments to foreign security forces, so no count exists. Also open: whether the payments caused particular killings. A Florida jury found Chiquita liable in June 2024 for eight killings, but Freeport denied the ACFOA death figures and Shell denies colluding with the Nigerian military.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The DOJ release in full, including the outside counsel's advice and the post-disclosure payments; every figure in the entry's first paragraph checks out against it.
Freeport's current 10-K, read for the Indonesia security-support disclosure. Note it gives no dollar figure, so the entry's $20 million for 1998-2004 still rests on the New York Times story.

routes_that_failed.how_it_failed: Served an Akamai interstitial challenge instead of the page, so the Lafarge plea was not confirmed from DOJ directly; web.archive.org returned 403 and the CourtListener API returned 401, so the plea rests on the entry's OCCRP, AP and NPR sources.

water-handed-to-companies.title_asserts: Cities' water systems were handed to foreign companies on the lenders' advice.
water-handed-to-companies.why: The World Bank's own Independent Evaluation Group counted the practice across its portfolio rather than in three cities: 13% of its urban water and sanitation projects aimed to bring in the private sector, 70 of those projects had closed, 46 had done it, and where the Bank's support succeeded, “the international private firms tended to become involved in urban areas”. That is the lender designing projects to hand city water to foreign operators, published by the lender's own evaluators. The cities in the entry are instances of a programme the Bank documented itself.

settled_by.what_it_is: Independent Evaluation Group, 'Water and Development: An Evaluation of World Bank Support, 1997-2007', World Bank publication
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Thirteen per cent of urban water and sanitation projects aimed to introduce private sector participation; of 70 closed, 46 involved the private sector as planned; Bolivia cancelled all its contracts and Turkey and Venezuela terminated theirs early; international private firms took the urban work while local firms took the rural work.

settled_by.what_it_is: World Bank Implementation Completion Report, Indonesia - Second Jabotabek Urban Development Project
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The Bank's own account of Jakarta calls the privatisation of PAM JAYA's operations “parallel to but facilitated by the Project”, while saying in the same sentence that it was not envisaged by the government or the Bank at appraisal; the two 25-year cooperation agreements took effect in February 1998, after which the foreign operators bought out their local partners.

water-handed-to-companies.still_open: Whether privatisation was imposed as a loan condition in any particular city - Cochabamba's $14 million conditioned loan rests on the Democracy Center, not on a Bank document I could open - and who the lenders consulted before advising. Note also that the entry overlaps the documented pattern 'company-sued-the-state', which already covers the arbitration claims that followed these concessions; the part that is new here is the lending and advice that came first.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: The IEG water evaluation, read for the private-participation chapter.
The 1998 Jabotabek completion report, read in full on the privatisation passages - including the sentence that qualifies the entry's use of it, see the report.
